newsitem.title: USA: Five oil companies fight U.S. MMS subpoenas.
newsitem.headline: Five oil companies fight U.S. MMS subpoenas.

text.p: Five oil companies subpoenaed last fall by the U.S. government have refused to hand over their oil sale records from 1980 to 1988, the U.S. Minerals Management Service said Thursday.
The records were sought in a dispute over whether the companies underpaid royalties they owed the U.S. government on oil they produced on federal land in California.

Chevron Corp, Mobil Corp, Occidental Oil and Gas Corp, ARCO, and Royal Dutch/Shell's Shell Oil are fighting the subpoenas, and "we expect them to begin court action soon," MMS Director Cynthia Quarterman said at a news conference.
Three other companies, Exxon Corp, Unocal Corp, and Pennzoil Co, had complied with the MMS request.
MMS last fall billed 10 companies for a total of $385 million in underpaid royalties off federal leases in California.
The oil companies argue that they have paid all the royalties they owed in the past, based on regulations that were in place at the time.
Under those rules, companies were expected to pay royalties based on the market value of their oil, which the government at the time said included companies' posted prices.
But following a two-year study, MMS last year found that companies had sold their oil at premiums to posted prices.
"They paid us (based on) one thing, then paid themselves above that," said Robert Armstrong, assistant secretary for land and minerals management.
Sen. Barbara Boxer, D-Calif., accused the companies of trying to get out of what they truly owe and depriving California of about $75 million for public schools.
California receives 50 percent of royalties collected from federal leases in the state.
"It is outrageous that ... deadbeat oil companies still have not paid the bills sent to them by the federal government," she said at the news conference.
"If the companies would open their books we could solve this," she said, adding that Shell, Mobil, Marathon, and Oryx Energy Co were the worst offenders.
ARCO denied it had failed to cooperate with the October subpoena. "We are working with the auditors to provide the documents they have requested," said spokesman Al Greenstein.
A spokeswoman for OXY USA Inc said Occidental had refused to reopen its books because it had been audited from 1977 through 1992 and settled all royalty issues for that period.
"What we're challenging is what was previously audited and what was previously settled," said OXY's Patricia Patton.
Mobil spokesman Chris Springham said the company had cooperated with the government but "we've challenged certain actions because they are beyond the legal authority."

Quarterman said some companies argued that MMS had no right to reopen records because they were beyond the statute of limitations. But the agency believes there is no time limit for recovering royalties due in the past.

The agency recently issued a proposal to change the way companies calculate their royalties, calling for payments to be based on oil futures prices and, in California on prices for Alaskan crude, instead of posted prices.
Shell and Chevron were not immediately available to comment on compliance with the subpoenas, but both companies have said in the past they believe they have fully paid the royalties they owed.
